\chapter{How Are You?}
\label{ch:responding}
\hlchaptermodality{3}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask how someone is in Punjabi, answer naturally, and return the question.}

Complete separate oral listening and speaking checks: understand a respectful wellbeing question, answer naturally, return the question, and close a thanks exchange. Independent Gurmukhi reading and writing remain blocked until \#13068 teaches the forms.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kivēṁ]{\pa{ਕਿਵੇਂ} (kivēṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}how,\textquotedblright{} another of the k- questions}

\label{lesson:PA-C03-kivein}



\begin{quote}
You met \textbf{\pa{ਕੀ}} (\emph{kī}, \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}) in Chapter 2. Here is its sibling — and, like all of Punjabi's question-words, it starts with \textbf{k-}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਕ}} (\emph{ka}) + \textbf{\pa{ਿ}} (the \emph{sihārī}, \emph{i}-sign, written before) $\to$ \textbf{\pa{ਕਿ}} (\emph{ki}); \textbf{\pa{ਵ}} (\emph{va}) + \textbf{\pa{ੇ}} (\emph{e}-sign) + \textbf{\pa{ਂ}} (nasal) $\to$ \textbf{\pa{ਵੇਂ}} (\emph{vēṁ}). Read \textbf{\pa{ਕਿ}·\pa{ਵੇਂ}} $\to$ \emph{kivēṁ}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਕਿਵੇਂ}} (\emph{kivēṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{}) is from the interrogative stem \textbf{ka-}, from PIE \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-} — the same question-root behind English \textbf{wh-} and Latin \emph{qu-}. Punjabi's questions nearly all begin with this \textbf{k-}: \emph{kī} (what), \emph{kauṇ} (who), \emph{kad} (when), \emph{kithē} (where), \emph{kivēṁ} (how). Learn the \emph{k-} and you can spot a question.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kivēṁ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the k- question family — \emph{kī, kauṇ, kad, kithē, kivēṁ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What root do Punjabi's question-words share, and its English family? (The interrogative \emph{k-}, PIE \emph{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-}; the \emph{wh-} words.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tusī̃ kivēṁ ho?]{\pa{ਤੁਸੀਂ} \pa{ਕਿਵੇਂ} \pa{ਹੋ}? (tusī̃ kivēṁ ho?) — \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PA-C03-tusi-kivein-ho}



\begin{quote}
Three words you own, assembled into the first thing you ask after hello.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਤੁਸੀਂ} \pa{ਕਿਵੇਂ} \pa{ਹੋ}?} = \textbf{\pa{ਤੁਸੀਂ}} (\emph{tusī̃}, respectful \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\pa{ਕਿਵੇਂ}} (\emph{kivēṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\pa{ਹੋ}} (\emph{ho}, \textquotedblleft{}are\textquotedblright{}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{you how are?}\textquotedblright{} Punjabi keeps the verb \textbf{last}, as in Chapter 2. The copula \emph{ho} is the respectful \textquotedblleft{}are\textquotedblright{} that goes with \emph{tusī̃} — its whole set is \emph{maiṁ hāṁ} (I am), \emph{tū̃ haiṁ} (you are, familiar), \emph{oh hai} (he is), \emph{tusī̃ ho} (you are, respectful).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: match the \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} to the verb}]
To an elder or stranger: \textbf{\pa{ਤੁਸੀਂ} \pa{ਕਿਵੇਂ} \pa{ਹੋ}?} To a friend (\emph{tū̃}): \textbf{\pa{ਤੂੰ} \pa{ਕਿਵੇਂ} \pa{ਹੈਂ}?} (\emph{tū̃ kivēṁ haiṁ?}). Respect takes the plural-shaped \emph{tusī̃ … ho}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the respectful question — \emph{tusī̃ kivēṁ ho?}
  \item the familiar version — \emph{tū̃ kivēṁ haiṁ?}
  \item where the verb sits (at the end)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} respectfully, and say where the verb goes. (\emph{Tusī̃ kivēṁ ho?}; the verb is last.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[maiṁ]{\pa{ਮੈਂ} (maiṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} the m- of the first person}

\label{lesson:PA-C03-main}



\begin{quote}
To answer \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} you first need \textquotedblleft{}I.\textquotedblright{} In Chapter 2 you learned \emph{merā} (\textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}); here is its owner.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਮ}} (\emph{ma}) + \textbf{\pa{ੈ}} (\emph{ai}-sign) + \textbf{\pa{ਂ}} (nasal \emph{bindi}) $\to$ \textbf{\pa{ਮੈਂ}} (\emph{maiṁ}). One nasal syllable.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਮੈਂ}} (\emph{maiṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) is on the first-person root \textbf{ma-} — the same root that gave you \emph{merā} (\textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}), and the same \textbf{m-} behind English \textbf{me}, \textbf{my}, \textbf{mine} and Latin \emph{mē}. Punjabi's \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} its \textquotedblleft{}my,\textquotedblright{} and English's \textquotedblleft{}me/my\textquotedblright{} all grow from one ancient first-person sound.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the copula pairs with it}]
\emph{Maiṁ} takes the copula \textbf{\pa{ਹਾਂ}} (\emph{hāṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}am\textquotedblright{}): \emph{maiṁ … hāṁ}. Watch out — this \emph{hāṁ} (\textquotedblleft{}am\textquotedblright{}) is spelled the same as the \emph{hāṁ} (\textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}) from Chapter 1; context tells them apart. So the reply to \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} will begin \emph{maiṁ …}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}maiṁ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the m- family — \emph{maiṁ} (I), \emph{merā} (my), English \emph{me}, \emph{my}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}maiṁ … hāṁ\textquotedblright{} — I am …
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What root links \emph{maiṁ}, \emph{merā}, and English \emph{me}, and what copula does \emph{maiṁ} take? (The first-person \emph{ma-}; \emph{hāṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}am.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṭhīk]{\pa{ਠੀਕ} (ṭhīk) — \textquotedblleft{}fine,\textquotedblright{} and how to answer}

\label{lesson:PA-C03-thik}



\begin{quote}
The word that answers \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} — and does a dozen other jobs.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਠ}} (\emph{ṭha}, a \textbf{retroflex} \emph{th} — tongue curled to the roof of the mouth) + \textbf{\pa{ੀ}} (long \emph{ī}) + \textbf{\pa{ਕ}} (\emph{ka}) $\to$ \textbf{\pa{ਠੀਕ}} (\emph{ṭhīk}). The retroflex \pa{ਟ}-\pa{ਠ}-\pa{ਡ} series is a hallmark of Indian sound.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਠੀਕ}} (\emph{ṭhīk}) means \textquotedblleft{}correct, right, fine, OK\textquotedblright{} — a native Indian word (shared with Hindi and Urdu), one of the most useful in the language: \emph{ṭhīk hai} (\textquotedblleft{}OK / agreed\textquotedblright{}), \emph{sab ṭhīk?} (\textquotedblleft{}all well?\textquotedblright{}). Not every word has a far-flung cognate, and that is worth seeing too: \emph{ṭhīk} is Indian to the core.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the reply}]
Put it together: \textbf{\pa{ਮੈਂ} \pa{ਠੀਕ} \pa{ਹਾਂ}} (\emph{maiṁ ṭhīk hāṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I am fine}\textquotedblright{} (literally \textquotedblleft{}I fine am,\textquotedblright{} verb last). Add thanks: \emph{maiṁ ṭhīk hāṁ, dhannavād.} The whole exchange:

\begin{quote}
— \emph{tusī̃ kivēṁ ho?} (\textquotedblleft{}How are you?\textquotedblright{}) — \emph{maiṁ ṭhīk hāṁ, dhannavād.} (\textquotedblleft{}I'm fine, thank you.\textquotedblright{})
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ṭhīk\textquotedblright{} — feel the retroflex \emph{ṭh}
  \item the full reply — \emph{maiṁ ṭhīk hāṁ}
  \item the casual \textquotedblleft{}OK\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ṭhīk hai}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the reply to \emph{tusī̃ kivēṁ ho?} aloud. (\emph{Maiṁ ṭhīk hāṁ.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[koī gall nahīṁ]{\pa{ਕੋਈ} \pa{ਗੱਲ} \pa{ਨਹੀਂ} (koī gall nahīṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}it's nothing\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PA-C03-koi-gall-nahin}



\begin{quote}
When someone thanks you — or apologises — this is the easy, gracious reply, built on a word from Chapter 1.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਕੋਈ}} (\emph{koī}, \textquotedblleft{}any\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\pa{ਗੱਲ}} (\emph{gall}, \textquotedblleft{}matter, talk\textquotedblright{} — note the \emph{addak}, the doubling mark, on \textbf{\pa{ੱਲ}}) + \textbf{\pa{ਨਹੀਂ}} (\emph{nahīṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}not,\textquotedblright{} from Chapter 1) $\to$ \emph{koī gall nahīṁ}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਕੋਈ} \pa{ਗੱਲ} \pa{ਨਹੀਂ}} literally means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{{[}there is{]} no matter}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{koī} (\textquotedblleft{}any\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{gall} (\textquotedblleft{}matter, thing, talk\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{nahīṁ} (\textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{}). It serves as \textquotedblleft{}it's nothing / no worries / never mind / you're welcome.\textquotedblright{} The word \textbf{\pa{ਗੱਲ}} (\emph{gall}, \textquotedblleft{}talk, matter\textquotedblright{}) is a warm, everyday native Punjabi word — \emph{gall karnā} (\textquotedblleft{}to have a chat\textquotedblright{}). And \textbf{\pa{ਨਹੀਂ}} (\emph{nahīṁ}) you already met in Chapter 1: the ancient negative \emph{na-}, the same PIE \textbf{*ne} behind English \textbf{no}, \textbf{not}, \textbf{none}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}koī gall nahīṁ\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it literally means (\textquotedblleft{}{[}there is{]} no matter\textquotedblright{})
  \item the exchange — \emph{dhannavād} / \emph{koī gall nahīṁ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{koī gall nahīṁ} literally say, and which Chapter-1 word does it reuse? (\textquotedblleft{}There's no matter\textquotedblright{}; \emph{nahīṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} — from PIE \emph{*ne}, English \emph{no}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 3 — The how-are-you exchange}

\label{lesson:PA-C03-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. The whole responding cycle, from atoms you now own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}How are you?\textquotedblright{} (respectful) — \emph{tusī̃ kivēṁ ho?}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I'm fine, thank you.\textquotedblright{} — \emph{maiṁ ṭhīk hāṁ, dhannavād.}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}It's nothing / you're welcome.\textquotedblright{} — \emph{koī gall nahīṁ.}
  \item the familiar question — \emph{tū̃ kivēṁ haiṁ?}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn — the atoms}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the k- question-word for \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{} (\emph{kivēṁ})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} and its copula (\emph{maiṁ}, \emph{hāṁ})
  \item the homophone trap — \emph{hāṁ} means both \textquotedblleft{}am\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kivēṁ} $\leftarrow$ the interrogative \emph{k-} (PIE \emph{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-}), cousin of English \emph{how/what}
  \item \emph{maiṁ} $\leftarrow$ \emph{ma-} (PIE \emph{*me-}), cousin of English \emph{me/my}
  \item \emph{ṭhīk} — native Indian \textquotedblleft{}fine,\textquotedblright{} no European cognate
  \item \emph{koī gall nahīṁ} — \textquotedblleft{}no matter\textquotedblright{}; \emph{nahīṁ} $\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{*ne}, English \emph{no}
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
A stranger asks \emph{tusī̃ kivēṁ ho?} — give a full, polite reply, and answer their thanks. (\emph{Maiṁ ṭhīk hāṁ, dhannavād} — and to thanks, \emph{koī gall nahīṁ}.)

Independent Gurmukhi reading and writing are \textbf{not scored here}. Chapter 3 still contains untaught forms; \#13068 must build their visible-model, guided-copy, delayed-copy, and dictation runway before either skill can earn credit. A romanized answer never counts as Gurmukhi writing.
\end{tcolorbox}
